newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Reserves data fuels talk of S.African forex move.
newsitem.headline: Reserves data fuels talk of S.African forex move.

text.p: A surprise fall in South Africa's net official reserves in February may mean commercial banks increased their foreign exchange balances ahead of a move to ease exchange controls, economists said on Wednesday.
The South African Reserve Bank said late on Tuesday provisional gross gold and foreign exchange reserves amounted to 12.5 billion rand at end-February compared to 11.8 billion rand as at January 31.
But the figure was inflated by the bank's use of 2.1 billion rand of foreign credit lines.
Stripping out that loan, reserves actually fell by 1.4 billion rand -- a far worse figure than economists had expected given strong foreign capital inflows last month.

"I'm pretty sure there were net inflows of funds in February but I think the commercial banks increased their balance of foreign exchange," said Henry Flint, economist at stockbroker Mathison and Hollidge.
He said the central bank may have allowed commercial banks to increase their holdings of foreign currency ahead of the next step to relax exchange controls.
The authorities are widely expected to announce a move on controls in, or ahead of, next Wednesday's budget.
If that happens and residents are allowed greater access to foreign exchange -- perhaps via foreign currency accounts -- the banking system would need to boost its forex holdings.
Commercial banks would also need more foreign exchange if the central bank pushes ahead with further steps to withdraw from the forward cover market.
The Reserve Bank said only that it had taken the 2.1 billion rand loan to fund the redemption of a 250 million Ecu bond and to build the foreign exchange liquidity.
But this reasoning left many economists mystified.
"It really is a puzzle but it does seem to portend that something is in the works," said Tony Twine, economist at Econometrix consultancy.
Gordon Smith, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said increased forex holdings by banks was one of several possible explanations for the 2.1 billion rand loan.
It was also possible that the central bank had decided to frontload repayment of a $800 million drought relief loan, repayments of which start to fall due this month, he said.

The least plausible but most alarming explanation would be that the current account had deteriorated very rapidly to the extent that the Reserve Bank needed a loan, despite last month's strong foreign portolio investment, he added.

Nick Barnardt, economist at BOE NatWest, said he was concerned that there may have been further very high imports in February and the authorities may have felt they needed to take the loan to keep "headline" reserves high.
"I feel it could all be put down to confidence-building," he said.
